questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic by his mother, who is concerned about his frequent episodes of "daydreaming." She reports that during these episodes, which last several seconds and occur multiple times a day, her son appears completely disengaged and unresponsive to verbal cues. Outside of these episodes, the boy is described as attentive and capable of completing tasks without difficulty. His academic performance is satisfactory, and he is not known to be disruptive in the classroom. The mother is worried these episodes are affecting his learning and social interactions. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic by his mother, who is concerned about his frequent episodes of "daydreaming." She reports that during these episodes, which last several seconds and occur multiple times a day, her son appears completely disengaged and unresponsive to verbal cues. Outside of these episodes, the boy is described as attentive and capable of completing tasks without difficulty. His academic performance is satisfactory, and he is not known to be disruptive in the classroom. The mother is worried these episodes are affecting his learning and social interactions. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Obtain further information from his parents and teachers with the Conners rating scale.

options.label: B
options.text: Begin a program of behavioral modification.

options.label: C
options.text: Reassure the child’s mother that this behavior is age appropriate.

options.label: D
options.text: Send the child for an electroencephalogram.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought to a pediatric outpatient department with a 5-month history of rectal bleeding, characterized by fresh blood clearly visible on the stool. The boy reports no significant constipation, vomiting, diarrhea, or weight loss. His diet is typical for his age, and he is growing appropriately. On examination, his abdomen is soft with mild tenderness on the right side, and stool is palpable in the descending colon. A sentinel skin tag is observed in the perianal area, but no fissures are present. Complete blood count (CBC) is within normal range, and both X-ray and histopathological examination (HPE) of the bowel show no abnormalities. Considering the clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child arrives at the pediatric outpatient department in the morning with complaints of recurrent nosebleeds and noticeable fatigue.
